query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under service-like thermal and cyclic stress conditions, an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy develops atomic-scale chemical inhomogeneities—specifically, elemental segregation at the grain boundaries—that mediate local short‐range order and possibly nanometer‐scale intergranular precipitates, thereby reducing grain-boundary cohesion and promoting brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy with homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal aging and cyclic mechanical loading designed to simulate service conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated temperature and cyclic stress regimes that allow sufficient atomic mobility without inducing large-scale grain growth; comparison to control samples maintained at ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale segregation of selected alloying elements at grain boundaries that may nucleate transient, nanometer-scale intergranular precipitates or short-range order domains.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic or elevated temperature conditions, slight variations in local chemical environment combined with stress concentration drive segregation of certain elements to the grain boundaries. This localized change reduces the cohesive strength at the boundaries, facilitating brittle intergranular failure even though the overall alloy remains single-phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-synthesized state, the thermally and mechanically stressed alloy will exhibit a measurable reduction in toughness (i.e. a shift toward brittle behavior) without significant grain coarsening. Microstructural analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography) should reveal enhanced grain-boundary segregation and possible nano-precipitate formation.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties and homogeneous chemical composition of the as-synthesized, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected under service-like conditions (moderate-to-high temperatures with cyclic loading over extended periods) while still retaining overall single-phase character and not entering the grain coarsening regime typical of conventional alloys.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical stress or temperature thresholds for initiating grain-boundary segregation in these alloys are not well established; thus, the rate and extent of segregation and its direct correlation to toughness reduction are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same single-phase high-entropy alloy. Subject one set to controlled thermal aging and cyclic mechanical loading while keeping the other set at ambient conditions as a control. Post-treatment, analyze both sets for grain-boundary chemistry using atom probe tomography and assess toughness via standardized mechanical fracture tests.
measurements: Atom probe tomography to detect and quantify grain-boundary elemental segregation or nano-precipitate formation.
Fracture toughness measurements (e.g., impact or bending tests) to quantify any reduction in toughness.
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD) to confirm retention of single-phase structure and lack of significant grain coarsening.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the treated HEA samples do not show any statistically significant increase in grain-boundary segregation and/or none of the expected microstructural changes, yet still exhibit toughness degradation, or conversely if detectable segregation is observed without a corresponding reduction in toughness relative to the control.
